When can we call a mission a success? 🚀

Liftoff may be the most spectacular moment, but it’s only the beginning.

For Arianespace, success means delivering a spacecraft where it needs to be, with the right trajectory and the right conditions for separation.

Once the spacecraft has safely separated from the launcher, it can begin the next part of its journey, whether that means reaching its operational orbit, deploying its systems or travelling towards a much more distant destination.

That’s where our launch mission ends, and our customer’s mission begins.

#LaunchingAmbitions

🚀 Before a spacecraft can be launched, it first has to arrive at Europe’s Spaceport.

Travelling by sea or air in a specially designed transport container, the spacecraft is taken to the Payload Preparation Complex, where its launch campaign begins.

Inside a controlled clean-room environment, teams open the container and carry out a series of inspections to confirm that the spacecraft has arrived in the expected condition.

From there, Arianespace coordinates the different stages of the launch campaign through to liftoff.

#LaunchingAmbitions

Not every mission is meant to orbit the Earth. 🌍

Some need to go much further.

2 hours and 14 minutes with Ariane 5. 786 days exploring a comet. ☄️

Rosetta lifted off from Europe’s Spaceport aboard Ariane 5 on 2 March 2004, beginning a journey that would take it billions of kilometres across the Solar System.

After reaching comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko in 2014, Rosetta spent 786 days - almost 2 years and 2 months - alongside it, observing the comet up close and gathering an unprecedented wealth of scientific data.

Ten years ago, Rosetta’s extraordinary mission came to an end on the surface of the comet it had travelled so far to explore.

From just over two hours with Ariane 5 to more than two years studying 67P, one launch marked the beginning of an extraordinary scientific journey.

#LaunchingAmbitions

From the downcomer going into the stage 1 tank to stage 2 completing its wet dress rehearsal at Stennis, September brought progress across every discipline.

🔩 Build: The downcomer was installed into the stage 1 flight tank. The interstage completed drilling and was passed off to the Tender Loving Crusher ahead of structural testing. Engine production continues to ramp, with articles for flights 2 and 3 well into manufacturing.
🧪 Test: With all 13 engines installed, the thrust structure transitioned into integrated gimbal testing. At Stennis, stage 2 completed a wet dress rehearsal on the A2 stand, building towards the first hot fire test.
🏗️ Launch: The east lightning protection tower reached its full height of 530 feet, the east launch table structural steel is complete, and permanent 480-volt power has been energized at the pad.

LC-16 is taking shape.

✔️ Flame diverter installation is underway, built to redirect the immense heat, exhaust, and acoustic energy generated at launch.
✔️ Launch table steel is going up alongside continued work on the LNG tank farm and lightning protection system, raising the first sections of the 531-foot towers.
✔️ Inside the HIF, outfitting continues as the transporter erector upper strongback takes shape.
✔️ The engineering support building is officially open, giving the teams who will operate Terran R launch campaigns a new home on-site.

Hardware across the vehicle continues to advance through test.

📍 Long Beach, CA
The first stage downcomer completed its full acceptance test campaign. This flight-critical component, which routes liquid oxygen from the tank to the engines, is now cleared for integration.

📍 NASA Stennis, MS
Stage 2 is back in the hangar after completing cryoproof and COPV proof testing. Post-test inspections are underway ahead of Aeon V installation. A2 is being prepped for hot fire, with LOX farm flushes and heat exchanger activations. On the R stand, acceptance testing of flight 2 Aeon R engines is underway.

Terran R hardware is advancing across multiple fronts, with integration work progressing on stage one and production scaling for future vehicles.

✓ All 13 flight one Aeon R sea-level engines installed onto the thrust structure
✓ All nominal joiners and external stringers approaching completion on stage one  
✓ Both interstage barrels were painted and stacked to form the full structure  
✓ All flight two barrels complete, first circumferential friction stir welds executed on the flight two stage one tank  
✓ Flight three panel fabrication more than halfway complete
